analysis.one_liner: Caps interest and fees on consumer loans at 36% per year nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2025 by three Democratic senators and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to make it illegal for any lender to charge consumers more than a 36 percent annual rate once every fee is counted — interest, late fees, overdraft fees, credit insurance, and add-on products. Today, payday loans average about 400 percent annual interest, car title loans about 300 percent, and bank overdraft fees can work out to far more. The bill counts all fees toward the cap so lenders cannot dodge it by relabeling interest as charges, and it keeps stronger state caps in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income borrowers who use short-term or small-dollar credit: payday loan customers, car title borrowers, people who overdraw checking accounts, and customers of high-rate online installment loans. Under the bill, no lender could collect more than 36 percent per year all-in, and loans made above the cap could not be enforced — the lender would have to return principal, interest, and fees, and state attorneys general could sue violators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers using payday, title, and overdraft credit

how_it_helps.text: Sets a national maximum 'fee and interest rate' of 36 percent for consumer credit, counting interest plus late fees, overdraft fees, credit insurance, and ancillary product charges toward the limit [S2].

Provides that a loan made in violation of the cap is unenforceable: the lender must return all principal, interest, charges, and fees, and violations carry criminal penalties of up to one year in prison and fines of up to triple the accrued debt or $50,000 [S2].

Allows state attorneys general to sue violators and preserves stronger state rate caps, and closes the loophole that lets nationally chartered lenders export higher home-state rates into every state [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, car title lenders, online installment lenders, and banks that collect overdraft and late fees would lose what the bill's findings put at roughly $12 billion a year in overdraft revenue, $8.6 billion in storefront and online payday lending, and $3.8 billion in car title loans [S2]. Some borrowers who currently rely on high-cost credit might find that credit harder to get, since lenders that cannot charge triple-digit rates may stop making small short-term loans at all.

drawbacks.text: A binding 36 percent cap can cut off supply, not just lower prices: some lenders would stop making small-dollar loans rather than lend at a rate that may not cover their risk, leaving some cash-strapped borrowers with no formal option in an emergency.
Banks might respond to the overdraft-fee limit by ending overdraft coverage entirely rather than offering it cheaply, so transactions could simply be declined instead of covered.
The cap applies to all consumer credit, including credit cards whose rates and fees exceed 36 percent for riskier borrowers, which could narrow card access for people with low credit scores.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the upside is large: it ends fees that work out to hundreds or thousands of percent per year and makes over-limit loans uncollectible. The honest cost is that the cheapest to serve borrowers gain the most, while some higher-risk borrowers may lose access to small-dollar credit altogether rather than get it at a lower price. Whether that trade is worth it depends on whether affordable alternatives actually fill the gap, which the bill encourages but does not guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in September 2025 and has sat there since, with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill with Sens. Blumenthal and Whitehouse on September 11, 2025; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S4].
No further action appears in the bill's history — no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and Congress remains in session [S4].

The bill's findings state that consumers currently pay roughly $12 billion a year in high-cost overdraft loans, $8.6 billion in storefront and online payday loans, and $3.8 billion in car title loans, with payday rates averaging about 400 percent annual interest [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost lenders and banks collecting overdraft and late fees keep their current revenue streams untouched, because the bill has not advanced. Borrowers keep paying today's rates.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to set a national 36 percent all-in rate cap on consumer credit.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in September 2025 and has scheduled no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors are Democrats, no Republican has cosponsored, and the Republican-led Senate Banking Committee has taken no action.

industries.note: The cap would outlaw their core product: loans averaging 400 percent (payday) and 300 percent (title) annual interest that currently generate about $12.4 billion a year by the bill's own findings [S2].

industries.industry: Banks collecting overdraft and late fees
industries.note: Overdraft fees count toward the 36 percent cap, threatening roughly $12 billion a year in overdraft revenue; banks would have to reprice or eliminate the product.
Triple-digit installment rates are capped, and the bill explicitly counts paycheck-linked advance products toward the limit.
Prime cards generally sit under 36 percent all-in, but subprime and secured cards whose rates plus fees exceed the cap would have to be repriced or withdrawn, narrowing card access at the low end.

analysis.trajectory: With only three Democratic sponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action months after referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or vote in this Congress; the realistic path is that it dies in committee unless support expands sharply.
